vignette: Two years ago, Kavi was cycling home through their neighborhood when an unmarked sedan mounted the curb and three officers barked commands. Before Kavi could comply, they were flipped onto the asphalt, pinned by a heavy knee and dragged by the collar. The violence was absolute, stripping away any illusion of predictable safety. When Kavi later returned to work as a software engineer, the glass-walled open-plan office became a landscape of constant threat assessment. A delivery rider on a rental bike gliding past the lobby entrance instantly triggered a visceral jolt of adrenaline. This sudden physical reactivity automatically pulled Kavi away from their standing desk and toward the reinforced pillar at the edge of the server room, where they always positioned themselves to monitor the room’s sightlines. The memory of the restraint never formed a clear timeline; instead, Kavi would find themselves pushing the experience away the moment it began to surface, ensuring it stayed fragmented. Because the past refused to organize into a coherent story, the unresolved fear of that afternoon constantly amplified Kavi’s baseline threat response, turning ordinary office noises into potential alarms. As the months passed, the cognitive appraisals deepened alongside the hypervigilance. Kavi began to believe their understanding of how the world works had been completely shattered, certain that harm could emerge from anyone without warning. This conviction made Kavi deliberately block any attempt to reconstruct the event, pushing the fragments away before they could cohere into a narrative. The belief that strangers could read the violence off Kavi’s face further distorted daily interactions. When Kavi’s spouse or coworkers initiated what were meant to be lighthearted exchanges, the fear of harm automatically converted the dialogue into a potential threat. Similarly, moments of genuine relaxation became dangerous; feeling happy or relaxed felt like lowering a guard that had already failed once, which in turn reignited the initial physical alarm. The memory fragments, now constantly cued by these avoided emotional states, bled into the present as intense panic episodes that arrived with no visual anchor, which in turn heightened Kavi’s sensitivity to routine office encounters. Consequently, the appraisal that the environment was fundamentally unsafe hardened further, as every triggered moment confirmed the original shattered beliefs. In the daily rhythm of sprint planning and code reviews, the maintaining cycle tightened into a rigid routine. Kavi watched others closely during stand-up meetings, interpreting crossed arms or rapid footsteps as precursors to violence. This constant scanning drained cognitive resources and cemented the conviction that danger was always imminent. The resulting anxiety then made Kavi hypersensitive to workplace disagreements, transforming routine feedback sessions into overwhelming confrontations. Meanwhile, the inability to tell a clear story of what happened meant that each triggered episode felt like a fresh assault rather than a remembered one. The loop became a self-sustaining engine: threat monitoring fueled appraisals of exposure and harm, which dictated avoidance of happiness and conflict, which left memory unprocessed, which in turn kept the nervous system primed for others cycling past the office or any sudden shift in tone. Kavi sought help only after a sprint deadline collided with a panicked retreat to the stairwell during a team celebration, leaving colleagues confused and Kavi utterly exhausted. What brought them to the clinic was not just the fatigue, but a quiet desperation to untangle a past that refused to stay in the past. Kavi hoped to reclaim the ability to feel safe in their own body and to stop bracing for a violence that, while it had happened, no longer dictated every step forward.
